notes.text: This chapter focuses on Saul’s son Jonathan, who will become a friend of David. Jonathan’s act of trust in this chapter is sandwiched between two examples of Saul’s disobedience (chs. 13 and 15 ).
The **outskirts of Gibeah** may mean “the edge of the hill.” **Migron** may mean “threshing floor.” Court was often held under a tree ( 22:6 ; Judg. 4:5 ) or on threshing floors ( 1 Kings 22:10 ).
**Bozez** means “the gleaming one,” and **Seneh** means “the thorny one.”
Jonathan’s trust contrasts with Saul’s concern about numbers ( 13:11 , 15 ). **Uncircumcised** was a customary insult directed at the Philistines (see Judg. 14:3 ; 1 Sam. 17:26 ; 2 Sam. 1:20 ).

**if they say, “Come up to us**.**”** This would give Jonathan and the armor-bearer the opportunity to get into the Philistine camp at what was probably its most thinly protected point, without raising an alarm. The guards’ words in v. 12 suggest that an attack by these two lone men was unexpected.
The Hebrew “yoke” ( esv footnote) was a unit for measuring area.
**A very great panic** is literally “a panic of God” (see esv footnote), suggesting divine intervention.
Saul was in **Gibeah**, about 4 miles (6.4 km) from Michmash. His **watchmen** were probably stationed nearer, watching Michmash.

The **ark** had apparently been brought from Kiriath-jearim to be with the army for some special reason. Saul wanted **Ahijah**, who carried the sacred lots in the ephod, to cast the lots before the ark.

Some people called **Hebrews** had previously sided with the Philistines (compare 29:3 ) while others **had hidden themselves** during this time of war. Now that Israel is succeeding, both groups commit to fighting for Israel.
**beyond Beth-aven**. This battle seems to have driven the Philistines from the central mountain areas.
**so Saul had laid an oath**. Jonathan, of course, had not been present at the time.
**His eyes became bright** suggests renewed vitality (compare Ezra 9:8 ; Ps. 13:3 ).
**this day**. See v. 24 (“until it is evening”). The day began at sunset.

When evening comes (v. 34 ) and the people are once again free to eat (see v. 24 ), they are in such a hurry that they do not drain the **blood** properly from the animals they kill (v. 33 ). Eating meat with blood is strictly prohibited in the law ( Gen. 9:4 ; Lev. 17:10–14 ).

**he shall surely die**. Saul assumes that the Lord does not answer Saul’s prior question (v. 37 ) because of some unknown sin (v. 38 ). Just as it was Saul’s own poor decision to impose the ban on eating (v. 24 ), it is also his decision to kill the person, whoever it is, whose guilt has prevented the Lord from answering him.

**give Urim. . . . give Thummim. . . . Cast the lot**. The Urim and Thummim (or just Urim) are mentioned also in Ex. 28:30 ; Num. 27:21 ; Deut. 33:8 ; 1 Sam. 28:6 ; and Ezra 2:63 . They may have been two stones of two different colors, one representing a positive and the other a negative answer, that were kept in the “breastpiece of judgment” of the priest’s ephod (see Ex. 28:30 ; Lev. 8:8 ). They were the only legitimate means of directly seeking a “yes” or “no” answer from the Lord, apart from God’s speaking directly to people.

**Shall Jonathan die? . . . Far from it! As the Lord lives . . .** The people use the same oath that Saul used in v. 39 . They obviously think God spoke much more clearly in Jonathan’s victory than in Saul’s foolish oath (v. 24 ).
It is possible, but not certain, that **Ishvi** is a variation of the name Ish-bosheth ( 2 Sam. 2:8 ; he is called “Eshbaal” in 1 Chron. 8:33 ).
**Abner the son of Ner, Saul’s uncle**. Although it may not be clear from the text, Abner was Saul’s uncle.
